test_title: PYST 4: Selection Post (Matric Level) - GA (Held On 28 Jul, 2025 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Carnatic music is mainly practiced in which part of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Southern India**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Carnatic music** is one of the two main sub-genres of **Indian classical music**, the other being **Hindustani music**. It is primarily practiced in the **southern part of India**, encompassing the states of **Andhra Pradesh**, **Telangana**, **Karnataka**, **Kerala**, and **Tamil Nadu**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Southern India.***

• The system is fundamentally based on **Hindu traditions** and is relatively free from the **Persian** and **Islamic** influences that shaped **Hindustani music** in **Northern India** after the **12th century**.

• The foundation of modern **Carnatic music** was laid by **Purandara Dasa** (**1484–1564**), who is revered as the **Pitamaha** (Grandfather) of the genre. He codified the basic lessons, such as **Sarali Varisai** and **Alankaram**, which are still used by students today.

• The music is predominantly **vocal-oriented**. Even when played on instruments, the performance style aims to replicate the nuances of the human voice, a characteristic known as the **Gayaki** style.

• The core components of this musical system are **Raga** (the melodic framework) and **Tala** (the rhythmic cycle). There are **72 Melakarta ragas**, which serve as the parent scales from which thousands of other ragas are derived.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **The Trinity of Carnatic Music**: This refers to three legendary composers of the **18th and 19th centuries**—**Tyagaraja**, **Muthuswami Dikshitar**, and **Syama Sastri**. They all lived in the **Tanjore** region of **Tamil Nadu** and their compositions form the backbone of the modern concert repertoire.

• **Musical Instruments**: Common instruments used in **Southern Indian** classical recitals include the **Veena**, **Mridangam** (the primary percussion instrument), **Violin** (adapted into the system in the **19th century**), **Ghatam** (an earthen pot), **Kanjira**, and the **Venu** (bamboo flute).

• **Madras Music Season**: Held annually in **Chennai** during **December and January**, this is one of the largest cultural festivals in the world. It features thousands of performances by both established maestros and upcoming artists, drawing audiences from across the globe.

• **Composition Structure**: A typical **Carnatic** composition, known as a **Kriti**, is divided into three sections: the **Pallavi** (the thematic line), the **Anupallavi** (the second part), and the **Charanam** (the final stanza).

• **Geographical Divide**: The **Vindhya Mountains** are traditionally considered the boundary separating the **Hindustani** music of **Northern India** from the **Carnatic** music of **Southern India**.

**Important Points__**

• **Linguistic Diversity**: While the music is practiced across **Southern India**, the lyrics of the compositions are primarily in **Sanskrit**, **Telugu**, **Kannada**, and **Tamil**. **Telugu** is particularly prominent due to the prolific contributions of **Tyagaraja**.

• **Comparison with Hindustani Music**: While **Northern India's** classical music places a heavy emphasis on **improvisation** and the exploration of a raga's mood, **Southern India's** **Carnatic music** is more structured, with a greater focus on **fixed compositions** and intricate **mathematical rhythmic patterns**.

• **Sruthi and Laya**: In **Carnatic music**, it is often said that **Sruthi** (pitch/intonation) is the mother and **Laya** (rhythm) is the father, emphasizing the balance required between melody and time.
